question: If the front tire goes flat while riding, the handbook says the steering will feel:
choice_d: Loose and wobbly only at low speed
explanation: If the front tire goes flat, the steering will feel heavy; a front-wheel flat is particularly hazardous because it affects your steering.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.32, 'Tire Failure'

question: If the rear tire goes flat while riding, the handbook says:
choice_a: The front wheel will lock immediately
choice_b: The motorcycle will accelerate on its own
choice_d: The back of the motorcycle may jerk from side to side
explanation: If the rear tire goes flat, the back of the motorcycle may jerk from side to side.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.32, 'Tire Failure'

question: If either tire goes flat while riding, the handbook advises you to:
choice_a: Hold the handlegrips firmly, ease off the throttle, and keep a straight course
choice_b: Immediately apply both brakes as hard as possible
choice_c: Accelerate to reach the shoulder faster
choice_d: Let go of the handlebars to reduce vibration
explanation: If either tire goes flat while riding, hold the handlegrips firmly, ease off the throttle, and keep a straight course.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.32, 'Tire Failure'

question: If braking is required after a tire goes flat, and you are sure which tire is affected, the handbook says you should:
choice_a: Apply the brake of the flat tire only
choice_b: Gradually apply the brake of the tire that is NOT flat
choice_c: Apply both brakes as hard as possible
explanation: If braking is required, gradually apply the brake of the tire that isn't flat, if you are sure which one it is.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.32, 'Tire Failure'

question: If the throttle becomes stuck, the first thing the handbook advises you to try is:
choice_a: Immediately hitting the engine cut-off switch
choice_c: Twisting the throttle back and forth several times to try to free the cable
explanation: Twist the throttle back and forth several times; if the throttle cable is stuck, this may free it.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.32, 'Stuck Throttle'

question: If the throttle stays stuck after trying to free it, the handbook advises you to:
choice_a: Continue riding normally until it frees itself
choice_b: Apply full throttle to try to overpower the stuck cable
choice_d: Operate the engine cut-off switch and pull in the clutch at the same time
explanation: If the throttle stays stuck, immediately operate the engine cut-off switch and pull in the clutch at the same time to remove power from the rear wheel.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.32, 'Stuck Throttle'

question: A "wobble," as described in the handbook, is best described as:
choice_a: A sudden side-to-side shake of the front wheel and handlebars at any speed
choice_b: A gradual drift toward one side of the lane
choice_c: A vibration felt only in the footpegs
explanation: A wobble occurs when the front wheel and handlebars suddenly start to shake from side to side at any speed.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.32, 'Wobble'

question: If your motorcycle starts to wobble, the handbook advises you to:
choice_b: Grip the handlebars firmly without fighting the wobble, and close the throttle gradually
explanation: Grip the handlebars firmly, but don't fight the wobble; close the throttle gradually to slow down.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.32-33, 'Wobble'

question: Why does the handbook warn against applying the brakes during a wobble?
choice_a: Braking has no effect on a wobble either way
choice_b: Braking is the only correct response to a wobble
choice_c: Braking could make the wobble worse
choice_d: Braking will stop the wobble instantly
explanation: Do not apply the brakes during a wobble -- braking could make the wobble worse.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.33, 'Wobble'

question: If a drive chain slips when you try to accelerate or climb a hill, the handbook advises you to:
choice_a: Continue riding and ignore the slippage
choice_b: Immediately disassemble the chain on the roadside
choice_c: Accelerate harder to overcome the slippage
choice_d: Pull off the road and check the chain and sprockets
explanation: If the chain slips when you try to speed up quickly or ride uphill, pull off the road and check the chain and sprockets.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.33, 'Chain Problems'

question: If a drive chain breaks while riding, you will notice:
choice_a: An instant loss of power to the rear wheel
explanation: With chain breakage, you'll notice an instant loss of power to the rear wheel; close the throttle and brake to a stop.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.33, 'Chain Problems'

question: Engine seizure -- when the engine "locks" or "freezes" -- is usually caused by:
explanation: When the engine locks or freezes it is usually low on oil, so its moving parts can't move smoothly and the engine overheats.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.33, 'Engine Seizure'

question: If you suspect engine seizure, the handbook says you should first:
choice_a: Apply full throttle to try to clear the problem
choice_c: Squeeze the clutch lever to disengage the engine from the rear wheel
choice_d: Downshift repeatedly without using the clutch
explanation: Squeeze the clutch lever to disengage the engine from the rear wheel, then pull off the road and stop; check the oil.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.33, 'Engine Seizure'

question: If you are chased by a dog while riding, the handbook advises you to:
choice_a: Kick at the animal to drive it off
choice_b: Stop completely until the dog loses interest
choice_c: Swerve sharply back and forth to confuse it
choice_d: Downshift, approach the animal slowly, then accelerate away and leave it behind
explanation: If you are chased by a dog, downshift and approach the animal slowly; as you approach, accelerate away and leave the animal behind. Don't kick at it.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.33, 'Animals'

question: For larger animals such as deer, elk, or cattle, the handbook advises riders to:
choice_a: Brake and prepare to stop, since these animals are unpredictable
choice_b: Accelerate past them as quickly as possible
choice_c: Sound the horn continuously and maintain speed
choice_d: Swerve toward the animal to scare it away
explanation: For larger animals (deer, elk, cattle), brake and prepare to stop -- they are unpredictable.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.33, 'Animals'

question: If a thrown object such as an insect or pebble strikes you or your face protection while riding, the handbook advises you to:
choice_a: Immediately let go of the handlebars to check for injury
choice_b: Keep your eyes on the road and hands on the handlebars, and pull off when it is safe to deal with it
choice_c: Brake hard and stop in your current lane
choice_d: Remove your helmet immediately to assess the damage
explanation: Whatever happens with a flying object, keep your eyes on the road and your hands on the handlebars; when safe, pull off the road and repair the damage.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.34, 'Flying Objects'

question: Before pulling off the road to rest or check the motorcycle, the handbook advises you to:
choice_a: Stop immediately without any warning to traffic behind
choice_b: Simply turn off the engine while still in the travel lane
choice_c: Check that the roadside surface is firm, signal your intention, and check your mirror and make a head check
choice_d: Wait until you are completely out of gas before stopping
explanation: Before getting off the road, check the roadside surface, signal, check your mirror and make a head check before taking any action.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.34, 'Getting Off the Road'
